analysis.one_liner: Creates universal health coverage through an employer mandate plus a new public health insurance plan.
analysis.headline: The Pepper Commission universal-coverage bill spent nineteen months in House subcommittees without a hearing or a vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill required every employer to enroll its workers and their families in a qualified private health plan or in a new public health insurance plan, and created that public plan for everyone else, run like Medicare. It capped employee premium shares, limited annual out-of-pocket costs to $3,000, subsidized low-income enrollees, barred insurers from turning people away based on health status, and paid for the government's share with a surtax on individual and corporate income.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured Americans, who would gain guaranteed access to a public or employer health plan covering basic services including preventive care; employees, whose premium share would be capped and whose annual out-of-pocket costs would be capped at $3,000; low-income individuals, who would get subsidies to limit or eliminate premiums and cost-sharing; children, who would get full EPSDT screening, dental, vision, and hearing coverage; and people buying small-group insurance, whose plans would have to take all applicants, renew policies, and use community rating.

how_it_helps.text: Would have guaranteed health coverage for basic services, including preventive care, to nearly all U.S. residents through employer plans or a new public plan
Would have capped employee premiums at 20% of the plan's cost and limited annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing to $3,000
Would have provided low-income assistance limiting or eliminating premiums and cost-sharing for individuals below and up to twice the poverty line
Would have barred employment-related health plans from denying or limiting coverage based on health status, and required small-employer plans to guarantee issue and renewal and use community rating
Would have required full EPSDT services for children, including dental, vision, and hearing, regardless of how the child was enrolled

Would have extended funding through 2000 for immunization, tuberculosis, lead poisoning, migrant and community health centers, homeless and public-housing health services, family planning, and HIV programs

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would be required to enroll full-time employees and their families in a qualified health plan or pay into the public plan, including contributions for part-time and seasonal workers; and individuals and corporations, through a surtax on income tax liability to cover the government's share of program costs. Individuals would also pay premiums (capped at 20% of the plan's cost) and cost-sharing up to an annual limit, with low-income enrollees getting help.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, plus a broad income surtax

drawbacks.text: The financing would have been heavy: an employer mandate raising labor costs across the economy plus a surtax on individual and corporate income tax liability
It included an individual coverage requirement enforced through tax returns, with people who failed to enroll charged twice the premiums they would have owed
Coverage of mental health and substance abuse treatment was limited to 45 inpatient days and 25 outpatient visits per year
The bill preempted state laws restricting network plans and utilization review, favoring managed care arrangements whose effect on patient choice of providers was contested
Payment rules under the public plan would have been exempt from administrative and judicial review, limiting providers' and others' ability to challenge rates

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — guaranteed coverage, capped premiums and out-of-pocket costs, protection from denial based on health status — would have been large and broadly shared, which is why universal-coverage advocates put it forward. The costs were also real and heavy: an employer mandate touching most workplaces, an income surtax, and an individual requirement enforced with double-premium penalties on anyone who failed to enroll. The mental health limits and managed-care preemption were compromises that a fair critic could point to. The bill's core trade was paying for universal coverage through taxes and employer contributions rather than leaving tens of millions uncovered.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and their subcommittees for nineteen months and never received a vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on June 4, 1991, implementing the Pepper Commission's blueprint for universal health coverage
It was referred jointly to three House committees and, over the next nine months, to three separate subcommittees
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993
Five Democratic cosponsors joined in April 1992, but the bill never advanced in any of its three committees

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and the health insurance industry were better off: no employer mandate, no income surtax, no public plan competing for their business, and no federal standards requiring guaranteed issue or community rating. The uninsured gained nothing from this bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, and the chairs of all three House committees of referral were also Democrats who never brought the bill up.

industries.note: The employer mandate would have created millions of new enrollees routed through employer-based private plans, and small-group plans would have gained guaranteed customers under community rating. But the new public plan, run under Medicare rules, would have competed with private plans, and plans could not have denied or priced coverage based on health status.

Every employer of five or more workers would have had to pay for coverage or contribute to the public plan, and the government's share would have been financed by an income tax surtax. Small employers with fewer than 5 workers would have been permanently exempt.

Universal enrollment would have brought them millions of new paying patients and reduced charity care. The tradeoff: the bill used Medicare payment rates, capped what providers could charge some employer plans, and left payment rules largely outside judicial or administrative review.

The bill preempted state laws restricting network plans and utilization review, clearing legal barriers to managed care growth. Whether this served patients through lower costs or restricted their choice of doctors was the contested question.
